q.s: A 4-year-old girl has had three febrile urinary tract infections. Voiding cystourethrogram shows contrast flowing from the bladder up the left ureter into a dilated renal pelvis during voiding. Ultrasound shows two separate collecting systems on the left.
o: Failure of the ureteric bud to form
Failure of the ureteric bud to induce the mesenchyme
Early bifurcation of the ureteric bud, or two ureteric buds reaching the metanephric blastema
cl: contrast flowing from the bladder up the left ureter
q.ch: Recurrent pyelonephritis + VUR + duplex system → ureteric bud splits early.
q.tr: Duplex systems are strongly associated with reflux and obstruction.
q.q2: What is the embryologic basis of her duplicated system?
q.fc: Family pedigree; I-1 and I-2 are first cousins and carriers are marked with a dot

q.s: A couple who are first cousins lost their first son on day 2 of life to respiratory failure. He had massively enlarged kidneys with dilated collecting ducts, a flat face and clubbed feet, and his liver showed fibrosis around the portal tracts. Their family is shown, and they are planning another pregnancy.
e: Wrong. Risk that an unaffected sibling is a carrier.
Correct. Autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease.
cl: massively enlarged kidneys with dilated collecting ducts
a flat face and clubbed feet
q.ch: Infant with enlarged cystic kidneys + Potter + hepatic fibrosis + consanguineous carrier parents → ARPKD (PKHD1) → 25% recurrence.
q.tr: ADPKD presents in adults with cysts in cortex and medulla.
q.q2: What is the chance that their next child will be affected?

q.s: A 70-kg man loses 3 L of isotonic fluid from severe diarrhea. He drinks nothing.
o: Extracellular fluid only; osmolality stays the same
q.ch: Isotonic loss → ECF volume falls, osmolality unchanged → no water shift into or out of cells.
q.tr: The ECF is about 20% of body weight (14 L in a 70-kg man).
q.q2: Which compartment loses volume, and how does plasma osmolality change?

q.s: A 45-year-old man with oliguria has a urine Na+ of 40 mEq/L, plasma Na+ of 140 mEq/L, urine creatinine of 40 mg/dL and plasma creatinine of 4 mg/dL. His values are shown.
o: 2.9%; intrinsic renal injury such as ATN
q.k: Calculation of reabsorption and secretion rate
cl: urine creatinine of 40 mg/dL and plasma creatinine of 4 mg/dL
q.ch: FENa = (UNa × PCr)/(PNa × UCr) = 160/5600 ≈ 2.9% → >2% → intrinsic (ATN).
q.tr: FENa < 1% suggests prerenal azotemia.
q.q2: What is his FENa, and what does it suggest?

q.s: A 62-year-old man with heart failure has a markedly elevated BNP. His physician explains that BNP partly counteracts the renin-angiotensin system.
o: Dilates the afferent arteriole and promotes natriuresis via cGMP
q.ch: Ventricular stretch → BNP → cGMP → afferent dilation, ↑ GFR, natriuresis, ↓ renin/aldosterone.
q.tr: ANP comes from atria; BNP from ventricles.
q.q2: Which effect does BNP have on the kidney?

q.s: A 58-year-old man in DKA has a serum K+ of 5.6 mEq/L. He is started on IV insulin and fluids. Two hours later his K+ is 2.9 mEq/L and he has muscle weakness.
o: Increased renal K+ secretion from aldosterone
Insulin stimulates Na+/K+-ATPase, shifting K+ into cells
q.ch: DKA: insulin deficiency, acidosis and hyperosmolality shift K+ out; insulin therapy shifts it back in → hypokalemia.
q.tr: Replace K+ before or with insulin when K+ is low or normal.
q.q2: What explains the fall in potassium?

q.s: A 74-year-old man with metastatic squamous cell lung cancer is confused, constipated and urinating frequently. He has abdominal pain and bone pain. His serum calcium is 14.2 mg/dL and PTH is low.
q.ch: Lung SCC → PTHrP → hypercalcemia (stones, bones, groans, thrones, overtones) → short QT.
q.tr: Hypocalcemia prolongs the QT interval.
q.q2: Which finding is also expected on ECG?
q.fc: Findings in two patients with metabolic alkalosis

q.s: Two patients have metabolic alkalosis. Patient 1 has had persistent vomiting from pyloric obstruction. Patient 2 has an adrenal mass. Their findings are shown.
o: Patient 2 is saline-responsive because aldosterone is high
Patient 1 has a low renin state
Patient 1 is saline-responsive (urine Cl− <20); patient 2 is saline-resistant
q.ch: Low urine Cl− + volume depletion → saline-responsive (vomiting); high urine Cl− + hypertension + low renin → saline-resistant (primary aldosteronism).
q.tr: Current diuretic use also gives a high urine Cl−.
q.q2: Which statement is correct?

q.s: A 64-year-old man with severe COPD has a pH of 7.34, PCO2 of 62 mm Hg and HCO3− of 33 mEq/L. He has been stable at this level for months.
o: Chronic respiratory acidosis with renal compensation
cl: stable at this level for months
q.ch: CO2 retention → respiratory acidosis → delayed renal HCO3− reabsorption → partially compensated chronic respiratory acidosis.
q.tr: Renal compensation takes days.
q.q2: Which statement best describes his acid-base status?
q.fc: Arterial blood gas and serum chemistry 4 hours after ingestion

q.s: A 22-year-old woman took a large number of aspirin tablets 4 hours ago. She has ringing in her ears, nausea and rapid breathing. Her results are shown.
o: Respiratory alkalosis plus anion gap metabolic acidosis
Normal anion gap metabolic acidosis only
e: Wrong. Gap high and pH alkalemic.
cl: took a large number of aspirin tablets
q.ch: Salicylates stimulate breathing early (respiratory alkalosis) and later cause AG metabolic acidosis; alkalemic pH with AG 22 → mixed disorder.
q.tr: Aspirin is the A in GOLDMARK (late effect).
q.q2: Which acid-base disturbances are present?

q.s: A 66-year-old woman with back pain, anemia and hypercalcemia has a monoclonal spike on serum electrophoresis. She also has glucosuria with normal blood glucose, phosphaturia and a non-anion gap metabolic acidosis. Urine pH is 5.2 when her bicarbonate is low.
e: Correct. Light chains damage the PCT (Fanconi syndrome).
cl: glucosuria with normal blood glucose, phosphaturia
Urine pH is 5.2 when her bicarbonate is low
q.ch: Myeloma light chains → PCT damage → Fanconi → proximal RTA (urine can acidify once HCO3− falls below threshold).
q.tr: Type 2 RTA increases the risk of hypophosphatemic rickets.
q.q2: Which type of renal tubular acidosis does she have?

q.s: A 52-year-old man eats several bags of black licorice every day. He has a BP of 168/100 mm Hg, serum K+ of 2.8 mEq/L and metabolic alkalosis. Renin and aldosterone are both low.
o: Inhibition of 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase, allowing cortisol to activate mineralocorticoid receptors
cl: Renin and aldosterone are both low
q.ch: Licorice → glycyrrhetinic acid blocks 11β-HSD → cortisol acts as mineralocorticoid → acquired syndrome of apparent mineralocorticoid excess.
q.tr: Treat by stopping licorice; K+-sparing diuretics help.
q.q2: What is the mechanism?

q.s: A 21-year-old man has visible red urine that began 1 day after he developed a sore throat. He had a similar episode with a cold 2 years ago. Serum C3 is normal. Biopsy shows mesangial proliferation.
cl: 1 day after he developed a sore throat
similar episode with a cold 2 years ago
q.ch: Hematuria during mucosal infection + normal C3 + mesangial proliferation → IgA nephropathy → mesangial IgA.
q.tr: Also the renal lesion of IgA vasculitis.
q.q2: What would immunofluorescence show?

q.s: A 26-year-old woman has a malar rash, joint pain and new leg swelling. Her results are shown. A kidney biopsy shows thickened capillary walls that look like stiff wire loops.
e: Wrong. Milder lupus class or IgA.
q.ch: SLE + nephritic-nephrotic syndrome + low complement + wire loops → diffuse proliferative GN → subendothelial deposits.
q.tr: "Wire lupus."
q.q2: Where are the immune complexes mainly deposited?

q.s: A 50-year-old man with untreated hepatitis C has edema, hematuria and protein of 5 g/day. Biopsy shows lobular glomeruli with mesangial ingrowth and a "tram-track" double contour of the GBM. Serum complement is low.
q.ch: HCV + nephritic-nephrotic syndrome + tram-track GBM → immune complex MPGN → subendothelial deposits.
q.tr: Dense deposit disease is complement mediated.
q.q2: Which deposits are seen on electron microscopy?

q.s: A 34-year-old Black man with untreated HIV has heavy proteinuria and edema. His kidneys appear large and echogenic on ultrasound. Biopsy shows collapse and sclerosis of parts of some glomeruli.
cl: sclerosis of parts of some glomeruli
q.ch: HIV + nephrotic syndrome + segmental sclerosis → FSGS (collapsing variant).
q.tr: Also linked to sickle cell disease and obesity.
q.q2: Which diagnosis is most likely?

q.s: A 60-year-old man with long-standing poorly controlled rheumatoid arthritis has nephrotic-range proteinuria and an enlarged liver. A fat pad biopsy shows apple-green birefringence with Congo red under polarized light.
e: Correct. AA amyloidosis from chronic inflammation.
q.ch: Chronic inflammation → serum amyloid A → AA amyloidosis → nephrotic syndrome.
q.tr: The kidney is the most commonly involved organ.
q.q2: Which protein is deposited?

q.s: A 14-year-old boy has passed several kidney stones since age 8. His sister has the same problem. His results are shown.
o: High fluid intake, urine alkalinization and, if refractory, tiopronin
cl: passed several kidney stones since age 8
His sister has the same problem
q.ch: Hexagonal crystals + positive nitroprusside + COLA aminoaciduria → cystinuria (PCT transporter defect) → fluids, alkalinization, chelation.
q.tr: "Sixtine" stones have six sides.
q.q2: Which treatment helps prevent his stones?

q.s: A 40-year-old woman had a large segment of ileum resected for Crohn disease. She has chronic fatty diarrhea and now has recurrent kidney stones made of calcium oxalate.
o: Unabsorbed fat binds calcium, leaving more free oxalate to be absorbed in the colon
q.ch: Ileal disease → fat malabsorption → fat binds calcium → free oxalate absorbed → hyperoxaluria → CaOx stones.
q.tr: Low urine volume and hypocitraturia also contribute.
q.q2: Why is she forming these stones?

q.s: A 46-year-old woman with locally advanced cervical cancer has nausea and fatigue. Her creatinine has risen from 0.8 to 4.2 mg/dL. Ultrasound shows dilation of both renal pelves and calyces.
e: Wrong. Would not raise creatinine much.
cl: creatinine has risen from 0.8 to 4.2 mg/dL
dilation of both renal pelves and calyces
q.ch: Pelvic tumor compressing both ureters → bilateral hydronephrosis → postrenal AKI.
q.tr: Creatinine rises only if both kidneys or a solitary kidney are obstructed.
q.q2: Why is her creatinine elevated?

head: Finding
Result
rows: Absent ankle reflexes, stocking sensory loss

q.s: A 68-year-old man with type 2 diabetes for 20 years has trouble controlling his urine. His findings are shown.
e: Correct. Overflow incontinence from neurogenic bladder.
q.ch: Diabetic neuropathy → detrusor underactivity → large PVR → overflow incontinence → catheterization.
q.tr: Anticholinergics are for urgency incontinence and worsen retention.
q.q2: What is the best initial management?

q.s: A 20-year-old woman has dysuria and frequency. Urinalysis shows many white cells and is nitrite negative. Gram stain shows gram-positive cocci in clusters, and the organism is coagulase negative and resistant to novobiocin.
q.ch: Young woman + cystitis + nitrite-negative gram-positive clusters, coagulase negative, novobiocin resistant → S saprophyticus.
q.tr: E coli is still the most common cause in this group.
q.q2: Which organism is responsible?

q.s: A 24-year-old woman at 28 weeks' gestation has fever of 39°C, chills, nausea and right flank tenderness. Urine has many white cells and white cell casts.
o: Progesterone relaxes ureteral smooth muscle and the uterus compresses the ureters
q.ch: Pregnancy (↓ ureteral tone, compression) + fever + flank pain + WBC casts → acute pyelonephritis.
q.tr: Screen and treat asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy.
q.q2: Why is she at increased risk for this infection?

q.s: A 10-year-old girl with recurrent febrile UTIs since infancy has hypertension. Imaging shows small kidneys with deep, coarse, uneven scars over blunted calyces. Biopsy shows tubules filled with pink casts that look like thyroid follicles.
cl: deep, coarse, uneven scars over blunted calyces
q.ch: Childhood VUR → recurrent pyelonephritis → coarse asymmetric scars, blunted calyces, thyroidization → chronic pyelonephritis.
q.tr: Chronic obstructing stones can also cause it.
q.q2: What is the predisposing condition?

q.s: A 30-year-old man with sickle cell trait has painless gross hematuria. He passes small pieces of tissue in his urine. CT urography shows ring shadows at the tips of the medullary pyramids.
q.ch: Sickle cell trait + gross hematuria + sloughed tissue → renal papillary necrosis.
q.tr: "SAAD papa": Sickle cell, Acute pyelonephritis, Analgesics, Diabetes.
q.q2: Which diagnosis is most likely?
q.fc: Daily urine output after the injury; dashed line = day 18

q.s: A 28-year-old man was trapped under rubble for 10 hours. He developed dark urine, a very high creatine kinase and acute kidney injury. His urine output over the following weeks is shown.
e: Correct. Polyuric recovery phase of ATN.
cl: dark urine, a very high creatine kinase
q.ch: Myoglobinuric ATN → oliguric maintenance phase (1–3 weeks) → polyuric recovery → hypokalemia and electrolyte wasting.
q.tr: In the oliguric phase the risks are hyperkalemia, acidosis and uremia.
q.q2: Which complication is most likely around day 18?

q.s: A 31-year-old woman has a placental abruption with massive bleeding and DIC. After delivery she makes no urine. CT shows that the outer cortex of both kidneys does not enhance, while the medulla does.
cl: outer cortex of both kidneys does not enhance
q.ch: Obstetric catastrophe + DIC + vasospasm → bilateral cortical infarction → diffuse cortical necrosis.
q.tr: Also associated with septic shock.
q.q2: What is the diagnosis?

q.s: A 64-year-old man with CKD stage 5 who refuses dialysis has sharp chest pain that improves when he sits up and leans forward. A friction rub is heard. He also has a flapping tremor of the hands.
cl: improves when he sits up and leans forward
q.ch: ESRD without dialysis + pericarditis + asterixis → uremia → dialysis (AEIOU).
q.tr: Uremia: Pericarditis, Encephalopathy, Anorexia, Nausea.
q.q2: Which treatment is indicated?

q.s: A 35-year-old man has progressive CKD and has always urinated large volumes of dilute urine. His father and grandmother needed dialysis in their 40s. Ultrasound shows small kidneys without visible cysts.
o: Autosomal dominant tubulointerstitial kidney disease (medullary cystic disease)
cl: always urinated large volumes of dilute urine
q.ch: AD inheritance + concentrating defect + small kidneys → ADTKD (medullary cystic disease).
q.tr: Poor prognosis.
q.q2: Which diagnosis is most likely?

q.s: A 32-year-old woman has severe hypertension that began 1 year ago. She has an abdominal bruit. Angiography shows a "string of beads" pattern in the middle and distal right renal artery.
cl: middle and distal right renal artery
q.ch: Young woman + hypertension + distal string-of-beads renal artery → fibromuscular dysplasia.
q.tr: Most common cause of secondary hypertension in adults is renal artery stenosis.
q.q2: Which diagnosis is most likely?

q.s: A 60-year-old man has a 4-cm renal mass found on CT for abdominal pain. It is well circumscribed with a central scar. Histology after resection shows large eosinophilic cells full of mitochondria without perinuclear clearing.
o: It is benign and arises from the collecting duct
It is malignant and arises from the PCT
It is associated with WT1 deletion
cl: well circumscribed with a central scar
large eosinophilic cells full of mitochondria
q.ch: Central scar + eosinophilic mitochondria-rich cells without perinuclear halo → oncocytoma (benign, collecting duct).
q.tr: Often resected because it cannot be distinguished from RCC on imaging.
q.q2: Which statement about this tumor is correct?

q.s: A newborn boy is large for gestational age with a big tongue, an omphalocele and one leg longer than the other. He has hypoglycemia on day 1.
cl: one leg longer than the other
q.ch: Macroglossia + omphalocele + hemihyperplasia + organomegaly → Beckwith-Wiedemann (WT2 imprinting) → Wilms tumor risk.
q.tr: Hepatoblastoma risk is also increased.
q.q2: Which abdominal ultrasound screening is recommended for him in childhood?

q.s: A 50-year-old farmer from Egypt who swam in irrigation canals as a child has painless hematuria. Cystoscopy shows a bladder mass, and biopsy shows keratin pearls and intercellular bridges. Eggs with a terminal spine are found in the bladder wall.
q.k: Squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder
cl: swam in irrigation canals as a child
q.ch: Chronic S haematobium infection → squamous metaplasia → squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder.
q.tr: "4 S's": Schistosoma, chronic cystitis, smoking, stones.
q.q2: What is the tumor type?

q.s: A 62-year-old man with heart failure has edema despite furosemide. He has a history of anaphylaxis to sulfonamide antibiotics. His physician switches him to a loop diuretic that is not a sulfonamide.
q.ch: Sulfa allergy + need for loop diuretic → ethacrynic acid → more ototoxic.
q.tr: "Loop earrings hurt your ears."
q.q2: Which adverse effect is more pronounced with the new drug?

q.s: A 58-year-old man with cirrhosis and ascites has taken spironolactone for a year. He complains of tender, enlarged breasts and decreased libido.
e: Correct. More selective mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist.
cl: tender, enlarged breasts and decreased libido
q.ch: Spironolactone antiandrogen effects → switch to eplerenone (selective).
q.tr: K+-sparing diuretics cause hyperkalemia and metabolic acidosis.
q.q2: Which change would reduce these effects while keeping aldosterone blockade?

q.s: A 66-year-old man with hypertension starts a once-daily pill. Three months later he has his first attack of gout in his big toe, and his fasting glucose has risen from 98 to 124 mg/dL. His serum calcium is slightly high.
q.ch: New antihypertensive + gout + hyperglycemia + hypercalcemia → thiazide ("HyperGLUC").
q.tr: Losartan is uricosuric.
q.q2: Which drug was started?

q.s: A 52-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes and albuminuria develops a persistent dry cough after starting lisinopril. She still needs a drug that protects her kidneys.
o: Losartan; it blocks AT1 receptors without raising bradykinin
e: Wrong. Not renoprotective in the same way.
cl: persistent dry cough after starting lisinopril
still needs a drug that protects her kidneys
q.ch: ACE inhibitor cough → switch to ARB (no bradykinin rise) → same renoprotection.
q.tr: Never combine ACE inhibitor, ARB and aliskiren.
q.q2: Which drug is best, and why does it avoid the cough?

q.s: A 38-year-old man with severe traumatic brain injury has rising intracranial pressure. He is given an IV drug that raises his serum osmolality and increases urine output.
e: Correct. Mannitol can cause pulmonary edema.
q.ch: Osmotic diuretic (mannitol) draws fluid into the vessels → pulmonary edema in heart failure or anuria.
q.tr: Also causes dehydration and sodium disturbances.
q.q2: In which condition would this drug be dangerous?

q.s: A 55-year-old man with hypertension is already taking lisinopril. A new physician adds a drug that directly inhibits renin. Within a week, his potassium rises to 6.2 mEq/L and his creatinine increases.
o: The renin inhibitor raises bradykinin only
Dual RAAS blockade (aliskiren + ACE inhibitor) increases hyperkalemia and AKI risk
The drugs cancel each other out
q.ch: Aliskiren + ACE inhibitor → dual RAAS blockade → hyperkalemia, ↓ GFR → avoid.
q.tr: Aliskiren is contraindicated in pregnancy.
q.q2: Why is this combination relatively contraindicated?

q.s: A 6-year-old child is evaluated for nephrotic syndrome that has not responded to steroids. The child also has ambiguous genitalia with XY karyotype and a unilateral flank mass. Biopsy of the non-tumor kidney shows diffuse mesangial sclerosis.
cl: nephrotic syndrome that has not responded to steroids
q.ch: Wilms + early nephrotic syndrome (diffuse mesangial sclerosis) + gonadal dysgenesis → Denys-Drash (WT1).
q.tr: WAGR is a WT1 deletion with aniridia.
q.q2: Which syndrome is this?
